995.title: How great thou art
995.hook: a Swedish poem that traveled from language to language into English
995.howItsDone: How Great Thou Art is sung by Christians of different churches, in congregations, at revival meetings, weddings and funerals, and it appears in hymnals in different languages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Flannery O'Connor, a book thrown across a waiting room, and your line was grace in odd places.

A summer afternoon on the coast of Sweden. A storm rolls in fast over the water: dark sky, lightning, thunder loud enough to shake the windows. Then, just as fast, it's gone. The air is washed clean. Birds start up again in the trees. Across the bay, church bells are ringing. That, the story goes, is what a Swedish poet named Carl Boberg saw and heard on his walk home. He went in and wrote a poem. It began, in Swedish, O store Gud: O great God.

Boberg's poem didn't stay in Sweden. It was set to a Swedish folk tune, and then it traveled. Tradition says it passed into German, and then Russian, before an English missionary heard it sung in Ukraine and made the English hymn now known as How Great Thou Art. The English words are modern and still under copyright, so they aren't sung here. But the hymn's bones are very old, and they're in the Bible. The poem moves the way the eighth Psalm moves. In the King James Bible: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" First the sky, huge. Then the small question: what are we, that you'd even notice? The hymn does the same. It sees the stars, hears the thunder, walks through the woods among the birds, and only then turns to the cross and to Christ coming home. Wonder first, then gratitude. And the refrain echoes older words. When King David hears a promise from God in Second Samuel, he answers: "Wherefore thou art great, O LORD God." A psalm says it its own way: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works!" Heard that way, the hymn keeps a simple order: look at what's there, then say so. Christians of different churches sing it, in different languages, at weddings and funerals and on ordinary Sundays. It started with a man walking home after a storm.

If you know How Great Thou Art, sing the first verse, quietly or out loud; if you don't, read the eighth Psalm's line slowly: when I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers. Then look closely at one made thing, a leaf, a stone, the lines of your own palm. If you pray, let the hymn's title be your whole prayer; if not, let that one thing hold your attention.
Boberg. Carl Boberg, the Swedish poet who wrote O store Gud, O great God, after a storm, the poem that became the hymn How Great Thou Art.
Your line: the air washed clean. After the thunder, the birds start up again. See you tomorrow.

996.title: The hospice
996.hook: Cicely Saunders, a Christian nurse and doctor, founds the modern hospice movement
996.howItsDone: Churches and Christian volunteers visit the sick and dying at home, in hospitals and in hospices, and chaplains of different traditions work alongside hospice nurses and doctors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Boberg, a storm over a Swedish bay and a poem that became a hymn, and your line was the air washed clean.

David Tasma is dying in a London hospital, far from Poland, where he was born, with almost no one to visit him. A hospital social worker, Cicely Saunders, sits by his bed. Over many visits, they talk about what a dying person actually needs. Not only medicine. Someone to listen. A place that feels less like a corridor and more like a home. Before he dies, the story goes, he leaves her a gift of money and says he'd like to be a window in the home she builds one day. She doesn't forget it.

Cicely Saunders worked first as a nurse, then as a hospital social worker, and then, because she saw that doctors wouldn't listen to her ideas about pain, she trained as a doctor herself. She was a Christian, and she spoke of her work as a calling. At the bedside she noticed that dying patients were often in pain that nobody was treating well, and lonely in a way nobody was treating at all. She came to speak of total pain: the body's pain, yes, but also fear, worry about family, money, and questions about meaning and God. Treat only the body, on her view, and you miss much of the person. So she founded St Christopher's Hospice in London, a place built for this: careful pain relief, nurses with time, families welcome, chaplains and gardens and windows. Tasma's window was there. Her conviction came down to something like this: you matter because you are you, and you matter to the end of your life. That's where today's carry comes from. It sits close to some very old words. In Matthew, Jesus tells of a king who welcomes people with these words, in the King James Bible: "I was sick, and ye visited me." And on his own last night, in the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus asks his friends: "tarry ye here, and watch with me." Not fix it. Not explain it. Watch with me. The hospice is a building where people keep watch.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`
`TARRY YE HERE, AND WATCH WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Think of someone near the end of life, or someone sitting by a bed tonight: a grandparent, a friend who is very ill, a neighbor in a care home; if no one comes to mind, think of the nurses and chaplains keeping watch tonight. If you pray, hold that person in the words watch with me; if not, keep them company in your thoughts. You don't need the right words.
The hospice. A place of care for people who are dying, shaped by Cicely Saunders, a Christian nurse and doctor, around the whole person: body, mind, family and soul.
Your line: you matter to the end. Staying counts, even when the words don't come. Day nine hundred ninety-six.

997.title: Jubilee 2000
997.hook: churches campaigned to cancel poor countries' debts, citing Leviticus 25
997.howItsDone: Churches and Christian aid groups campaign and pray for debt relief for poor countries, often drawing on the jubilee of Leviticus 25 and the line "forgive us our debts" from the Lord's Prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hospice: Cicely Saunders, and a place built to keep watch with the dying. Your line was you matter to the end.

Fifty years, then a trumpet. In the book of Leviticus, Israel is told to count seven times seven years, and then, on the day of atonement, to sound the trumpet through the whole land. What follows is a startling law. A field sold in a bad year goes back to the family that lost it. People who had sold themselves into service go home. Much later, churches and aid groups picked up that trumpet and pointed it at something modern: the debts weighing on poor countries. They named their campaign after the old law.

The law is in Leviticus 25. The fiftieth year is holy, and the King James Bible gives the command: "proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you." The reason comes a few verses on, spoken by God: "for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me." Nobody owns the ground forever. Everyone is a guest on it. Wealth can pile up for a while, but not for good. Deuteronomy has a smaller cousin of the idea: "At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release," a letting go of debts between neighbors. The honest part: some readers note that the rest of the Bible tells no story of a jubilee being kept. The idea traveled anyway. In Luke, Jesus reads from Isaiah in his hometown and announces "the acceptable year of the Lord," and some readers hear a jubilee in it. Christians who pray the Lord's Prayer in Matthew's words say: "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Christian groups, joined by people of other faiths and none, argued that old loans were pressing on countries that could barely pay for their own clinics and schools, and that a fresh start was owed. They gathered signatures, held vigils and marched. Some debts were later written off; others were not, and people still argue about what helped. But a line from an ancient law about farmland had walked into the rooms where finance ministers meet.
screen: `THE LAND IS MINE: YOU ARE GUESTS.`
`AN OLD LAW IN THE FINANCE MINISTRY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a debt, not only money, that has sat on the table a long time, and hold it without adding it up; then widen the circle to a country carrying something it cannot lift. If you pray, you can pray the line from Matthew, forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors; if you don't, just let the word release sit with you.
Jubilee. The fiftieth year in Leviticus, when debts were let go and lost land went home, the ancient law that named a modern campaign to cancel poor countries' debts.
Your line: proclaim liberty. The field goes home, and the land stays God's. See you tomorrow.

998.title: Food banks
998.hook: ordinary church halls feeding neighbors every week
998.howItsDone: Church congregations host or support food banks and community meals, collecting food at services, staffing distribution days with volunteers, and pointing to Jesus's words in Mark 6 and Matthew 25.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jubilee: an old law where the field goes home, and a modern campaign named after it. Your line was proclaim liberty.

Tuesday, four in the afternoon, a church hall that smells of floor polish and instant coffee. Folding tables in a row. Tins of beans, pasta, peanut butter, a crate of bread a bakery dropped off this morning. A retired teacher checks names on a list, kindly, without fuss. A teenager carries bags out to a car. A man in a work jacket studies the floor while he waits, until someone asks about his kids, and he looks up. None of this will reach a history book. And next Tuesday the tables go up again.

In Mark a crowd has followed Jesus to a lonely place, and it's getting late. The disciples suggest the sensible thing: send them away to buy bread in the villages. Jesus answers, in the King James words: "Give ye them to eat." Not, leave it to me. You. The disciples protest that they can't afford it. He asks what they have. "Five, and two fishes." The story ends with everyone fed and "twelve baskets full of the fragments" left over. Christians read that miracle in more than one way, but the order is plain: the hungry are handed to the disciples, and what they already have is where it starts. Then Matthew 25, a verse before the line the hospice lesson used. The king says: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." The people are puzzled. When? He answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Read that way, the man in the work jacket is not a project. In the story's terms, Christ is standing in the line. That changes the posture: a chair, a name, a question about his kids. Not every food bank is run by a church, and churches run them differently. Some hand out bags. Some set up a small shop where people choose. Some cook a hot meal and eat with their guests. Some Christians ask why the line is there at all: wages, rent, illness. Others say: feed today, argue tomorrow. Both are reading the same Gospels.
screen: `FIVE LOAVES: START WITH WHAT YOU HAVE.`

segments.voice: Open your kitchen cupboard in your mind and find something you'd be glad to eat yourself: not the dented tin from the back, but something good. Then picture the hall, the folding table, the line, one face. If you pray, you can pray for whoever will open that bag; if you don't, just hold them in mind kindly.
Food banks. Church halls and other places where neighbors bring food and hand it to neighbors, week after week, behind them the command in Mark: give ye them to eat.
Your line: give them to eat. Start with what you have. Day nine hundred ninety-eight, done.

999.title: The church in the south
999.hook: the typical Christian today is a young African or Latin American woman
999.howItsDone: Christians across Africa, Latin America and Asia gather in large cathedrals and small rented rooms alike, where young women, among others, lead singing, teach children and visit the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food banks: folding tables in a church hall, and the old command behind them. Your line was give them to eat.

Early Sunday in a West African city. A young woman irons a dress by lamplight, wakes her little brother, and walks him across town to a church that meets in a school classroom. She leads the choir. She teaches the children's class. On Wednesday she'll sit with a sick neighbor and pray with her. She holds no title. And yet some historians of world Christianity say that if you want one face for the church today, hers is a good candidate: young, female, African or Latin American.

Hold that next to an older picture of the church: stone cathedrals, pipe organs, northern winters. Historians who study where Christians live now describe the church's center of gravity moving south, toward Africa, Latin America and parts of Asia. They argue over the details and the figures, and this lesson leaves the figures to them. Some readers hear an echo of it in the book of Acts. At Pentecost, Peter quotes the prophet Joel: "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions". Daughters. Young men. The Spirit does not wait for age or rank. Paul writes to the Galatians: "there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." And in Acts the good news heads south almost at once. An angel sends Philip "toward the south", down the desert road to Gaza. A chariot passes, carrying an official from Ethiopia who is reading Isaiah aloud. Philip runs up beside it and asks, "Understandest thou what thou readest?" Before the chariot moves on, the man is baptized at the roadside water and goes on his way rejoicing. To some readers, a young woman in Lagos or São Paulo as a face of the church sounds less like something new and more like those earliest chapters. Churches differ on which roles women may hold: some ordain women as pastors and priests, some do not, and each side argues from scripture. This lesson ranks none of them. It only notices who keeps showing up in choirs, kitchens and Sunday classes.

Hold one young woman of faith in mind: a niece, a coworker, the girl who reads at church, or someone you'll never meet, walking to a classroom church on another continent this Sunday. Picture her morning, the iron, the walk, the songs. If you pray, you can pray for her strength and her joy; if you don't, just wish her well, steadily.
Lagos. A West African city whose young women, historians say, are one face of today's church, as Christianity's center of gravity moves south.
Your line: she is the church. Your daughters shall prophesy. Until tomorrow.

1000.title: The thousandth morning
1000.hook: a thousand days of a few minutes each: the long story you've joined
1000.howItsDone: Some Christians keep a short daily time of prayer or reading, often in the morning, and some pray set psalms at fixed hours, as monks and nuns do, returning to the same words day after day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lagos: a young woman leading a choir in a classroom church, and the church's center moving south. Your line was she is the church.

The first word on this path was amen: let it be so. Then came the stories, the practices, the long reading of the text. A second year opened with in the beginning, and let there be light. A third opened with a promise: I will not fail you. In between, mornings. Some on a bus. Some at a kitchen table before anyone else was up. Some missed or rested, and then a fresh start. A few minutes each. Stacked up, they reach a number worth stopping for.
screen: `AMEN. LET THERE BE LIGHT. I WILL NOT FAIL YOU.`

segments.voice: The Bible uses the word thousand in a few surprising places, and none of them is a scoreboard. Psalm 90 carries the heading "A Prayer of Moses the man of God", and it says to God: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night." A thousand years, to God, is one night shift. The second letter of Peter echoes that line and turns it both ways: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." So a single morning can carry real weight, and a thousand of them are small in God's hands. Both at once. Psalm 84 weighs it differently again: "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand." Then Lamentations, a book of grief over a fallen city. In the middle of its grief: "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." That's the hinge. In these lines the faithfulness belongs to God, not to the count. The morning is new whether yesterday went well or not. A monk chanting the same psalms at dawn, a grandmother saying the same prayer at the kitchen sink, a commuter with headphones on a train: each is building a life out of small, repeated mornings. The long story this year has told was carried that way. Not by big moments alone, but by people who did one small faithful thing, and then did it again.

Let a few mornings from this path come back on their own, a word that stuck, a story, the place you were sitting when you heard it, without grading them. Then let one thank-you rise, for a person, a line, or the plain fact of having come back. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words or the psalm's, a day in thy courts is better than a thousand; if you don't, just let the thanks be there.
Lamentations. The book of grief that still says mercies are new every morning, the hinge this lesson turns on after a thousand days of small practice.
Your line: a thousand mornings. Each one new. That's day one thousand.

1001.title: Block close: the long story
1001.hook: from Joshua to Lagos, saints and sinners, and the thread holding
1001.howItsDone: Christians remember those who went before them in sermons, hymns, saints' days and family stories, sometimes reading Hebrews 11 and 12 on the 'cloud of witnesses'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lamentations: a thousand mornings, and mercies new every one of them. Your line was a thousand mornings.

Line them up, the way this year met them. Joshua at the edge of the river, told to be strong and courageous. Ruth gleaning at the edge of a field. Elijah on Carmel. Ignatius in chains on the road to Rome. Francis kissing a leper. Luther hidden in the Wartburg. Harriet Tubman going back, and back again. Bonhoeffer in a cell. Mahalia Jackson singing. A young woman in Lagos leading a choir. The year didn't hide the other faces: the burnings, the betrayals, the abuse. Saints and sinners, sometimes in the same person. So what runs through all of it?

The letter to the Hebrews has a roll call too. Chapter eleven names people who lived by faith: Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab. Then it speeds up, and the names get uncomfortable: "Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae". Samson, whose story is full of violence and bad choices. Jephthah, who made a terrible vow. Hebrews doesn't scrub them. It puts them in the line. Then it says something honest about all of them: they "received not the promise". They died before they saw how it ended. Chapter twelve turns to the reader: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight". A stadium, with the ones who ran before in the stands. That's what this year has been: a cloud of witnesses, flawed and faithful. But Hebrews does not say the thread is them. The next verse tells the runner where to look: "Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith". And near the end: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever." That's the claim Hebrews makes about the long story. The heroes don't hold it together; some of them nearly pulled it apart. What holds, in Hebrews, is the one the runners look toward, and in that reading he is the same at the river with Joshua and in a classroom church in Lagos. Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants would tell parts of this year's story differently, and some in it fought each other. Hebrews still puts the runner's eyes in one place.
screen: `A ROLL CALL WITH SAMSON IN IT.`
`THE SAME YESTERDAY, TO DAY, FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: Let the faces of this year pass by slowly, the prophets, the monks, the reformers, the singers, the nurses, the martyrs, the ones who failed, until one of them stays a little longer than the others. If you pray, you can give thanks for that life; if you don't, just hold the name with respect.
Witnesses. Hebrews' name for all who ran before, named in a cloud, pointing the runner's eyes not to themselves but to Jesus.
Your line: the thread holds. Tomorrow a new block begins, a year of feasts and saints' days. This block, closed.

chat.says: Church history has so many awful people in it. What actually holds it together?
options: Hebrews says the heroes don't; it turns our eyes to Jesus, the same yesterday and today.
Hebrews says the good people simply outnumber the bad, so it all evens out.
Hebrews lists only the blameless ones, so the bad parts don't really count.
chat.meaning: Hebrews puts flawed people like Samson in its roll call, then tells the runner to look unto Jesus, the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
